query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 that is homogenised in the single–phase BCC region, the subsequent phase stability at 600–1000 °C is governed primarily by the chemical driving force for Cr–Al–rich B2 (ordered bcc) precipitation that increases markedly once the Gibbs free-energy difference ΔG(BCC→B2+FCC) becomes negative; the transformation proceeds only when sufficient long-range diffusion of Cr and Al can occur. Thus: 1) if cooling is rapid enough to suppress long-range diffusion, the alloy remains a metastable single BCC solid solution to room temperature; 2) if diffusion time (either by slow cooling or isothermal hold/aging between 600–900 °C) is provided, the alloy decomposes into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 (Cr,Al-rich) plus disordered FCC (Co,Fe,Ni-rich).
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy homogenised 1 h at 1250 °C in a single-phase BCC solid solution and water-quenched to preserve the high-temperature BCC structure.
generation.intervention: Thermal treatment consisting of either (a) water-quench directly to room temperature vs (b) furnace cool at 10 °C min⁻¹ or (c) water-quench followed by isothermal aging at 700 °C for up to 24 h.
generation.conditions: Inert atmosphere (Ar) to prevent oxidation; identical sample geometry; identical surface condition; identical prior homogenisation.
generation.structural_mediator: Long-range diffusion–controlled partitioning of Cr and Al that produces coherent B2 nuclei inside the parent BCC matrix, followed by rejection of Co, Fe, Ni into an FCC matrix that forms by reconstructive transformation at the interphase boundary.
generation.mechanism: • Thermodynamics: The Al addition lowers the enthalpy of an ordered B2 (Cr,Al-rich) phase relative to disordered BCC. Once cooling brings the alloy below ~1000 °C, ΔG for B2+FCC versus BCC becomes negative.  • Kinetics: B2 precipitation requires substitutional diffusion of Cr and Al; if cooling is too fast, their diffusion distances are insufficient and the BCC phase is retained metastably.  • Structural pathway: B2 forms first by ordering of the BCC lattice; compositional partitioning then locally increases the driving force for FCC (L1₂-like) formation in CoFeNi-rich regions, completing the BCC→(B2+FCC) decomposition.
generation.predicted_outcome: 1. Water-quenched samples show a single BCC peak in room-temperature XRD, no extra reflections in electron diffraction, and hardness ≤300 HV.  2. Furnace-cooled or isothermally aged samples show (i) superlattice {100}B2 reflections in XRD/SAED, (ii) emergence of FCC peaks, (iii) nanoscale B2 precipitates in STEM-HAADF enriched in Cr+Al, (iv) concomitant increase in hardness by ≥150 HV over the quenched baseline.  3. The volume fraction of B2+FCC increases with either slower cooling or longer aging time, following classical nucleation-and-growth Avrami kinetics.
generation.baseline: Water-quenched, non-aged material that remains a metastable single BCC solid solution at room temperature.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis expected to hold for 5–9 at.% Al and 30–45 at.% Cr in Cr–Co–Fe–Ni–Al alloys; outside this realm, other intermetallics (e.g., B2–NiAl or σ-phase) or sluggish diffusion at <550 °C may dominate, invalidating the predicted behaviour.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of the hardness change and exact transition temperature for ΔG<0 are estimated; kinetic effects of possible short-range order above 900 °C not fully constrained.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of specimens with the initial state defined above. Apply the thermal treatments (a–c), then perform: (1) synchrotron in-situ XRD during cooling and aging to track phase evolution; (2) atom-probe tomography and STEM-EDS to map element partitioning; (3) Vickers micro-hardness testing. Compare results to predicted outcomes.
measurements: Phase fractions from Rietveld refinement of XRD
Local compositions of precipitates and matrix from APT/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If rapid water-quenching followed by room-temperature analysis already reveals >5 vol% B2 or FCC, OR if furnace-cooled/aged samples still contain <5 vol% B2+FCC and exhibit no significant hardness increase (<50 HV relative to baseline), the hypothesis is falsified.
